To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the shell evolution of nuclei with extreme proton-to-neutron ratio is governed by the interplay of the Coulomb force and the spin-orbit interaction, and that the shell evolution with temperature is governed by the Pauli principle.

(i) the evolution of shell structure with isospin, mass and temperature, (ii) the role of the continuum in nuclear shell evolution, (iii) the role of nuclear correlations and (iv) the role of isovector pairing in nuclear shell evolution are important for the understanding of the physics of exotic nuclei.
the shell structure of the atomic nucleus is determined by the competition between the mean-field and the correlations, which are in turn determined by the nuclear Hamiltonian.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic investigation of the nuclear shell structure and its impact on nuclear properties and nuclear astrophysics.

the development of a unified theoretical framework for the description of nuclear structure, reactions and dynamics in the whole chart of nuclei, including exotic nuclei, with the goal to provide a consistent description of the evolution of the nuclear properties as a function of the mass number, isospin and temperature.

the study of nuclear structure and reaction properties of unstable nuclei, with a special attention to the physics of astrophysical relevance, such as the r-process nucleosynthesis and the physics of supernovae explosions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, although the nuclear many-body problem is still far to be solved, the present state of the art is able to provide a rather reliable and quantitative description of nuclear structure and response in most of the cases of experimental relevance.
nuclear shell structure and nuclear matter properties are not only of fundamental interest, but also play a key role in astrophysics.

, despite of the impressive progress achieved so far in our understanding of exotic nuclear systems and their role in the astrophysical phenomena, we are still far from a complete and satisfactory description of their properties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shell model has become a predictive tool for the description of exotic nuclei.
, with a few exceptions, the present nuclear structure and reaction models are not able to describe the nuclear phenomena at the extremes of nuclear existence.
we are now able to describe the shell structure of exotic nuclei with an accuracy of a few hundred keV, and that the nuclear response functions can be predicted with an accuracy better than 10%.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the nuclear structure of the heaviest nuclei, as well as the properties of neutron-rich isotopes, can only be described by including the continuum and the effects of correlations beyond the mean-field approximation.

the nuclear structure and response of exotic nuclei is strongly influenced by a few low-lying single-particle states, which are in turn determined by the interplay of a few key ingredients, such as pairing correlations, shell structure, and effective interactions.

the shell structure of nuclei at the drip lines and in neutron star matter is determined by a delicate interplay of the nuclear mean field and pairing correlations, and that the nuclear shell structure is a robust phenomenon even in extreme conditions.
